R04-E-01: Neutrality has a poor reputation among people who think seriously about war. To its critics it looks like a refusal to choose, a way for a small state to sit out the great moral contests of its time while others pay the price of deciding them. On this view the neutral is a free rider at best and a quiet collaborator at worst, trading with whichever side is winning and calling its caution a principle. The charge is not baseless, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what neutrality has usually been for the states that practised it with any success. For a small country surrounded by larger ones, neutrality is less a moral posture than a strategy, and a demanding one. Its purpose is to remove the country from the calculations of its neighbours, to persuade each of them that the territory will never be used as a road or a base by the others. That persuasion does not come from declarations. It has to be earned through a long record of evenhanded conduct, through refusing favours that would look like alignment, and, above all, through an army strong enough to make occupation expensive. The neutral that cannot defend its borders is not neutral in any meaningful sense; it is simply unclaimed, and unclaimed ground in wartime is soon claimed. Seen this way, neutrality is not passivity but a continuous effort of a particular kind. The neutral state must be ready to resist whichever side violates its frontier first, which means it must arm against all of its neighbours at once rather than against one. It must also be disciplined in peacetime, since a single treaty of friendship, a preferential trade deal or a careless remark by a minister can be read abroad as a signal of where it would stand in a crisis. Few alliances ask as much of their members as this solitary commitment asks of a country that has chosen it. None of this guarantees success. Neutrality works only so long as the great powers judge that respecting it costs them less than violating it, and when a neutral's territory becomes essential to someone's war plans, even a well-armed and scrupulous record may count for little. Nor does the strategic defence settle every moral question; a neutral that profits handsomely from a war it claims to stand apart from invites the suspicion its critics voice. But the critics usually ask the wrong question. They ask whether neutrality is admirable, when the more useful question is whether, for a particular state in a particular place, it is the course most likely to keep that state's people out of a war they could not win.
R04-E-02: Few historical lessons are repeated as confidently as the one drawn from the settlement that followed the First World War. A harsh peace, the lesson runs, breeds resentment, and resentment breeds the next war; a generous peace, by contrast, turns yesterday's enemy into tomorrow's partner. The lesson is attractive because it joins morality to prudence. It tells victors that magnanimity is not only noble but wise, and that they can secure the future simply by being kind. It also offers a single, memorable explanation for one of the great catastrophes of the last century, and explanations of that kind are hard to dislodge once they have settled into textbooks and speeches. The trouble is that the record does not sort so neatly. Some severe settlements have held for generations, because the defeated party was too weak to overturn them and the victors remained willing to enforce their terms. Some lenient ones have failed, because the loser read leniency as a sign that it had not really been beaten and that a second attempt might succeed. What such cases suggest is that severity and generosity are the wrong variables to watch. A settlement lasts when its terms match the actual balance of strength, and when the powers that wrote it remain prepared to uphold it. By this measure, the worst settlement is not the harshest but the one that combines harsh terms with a weak will to enforce them. Such a peace gives the defeated every reason to resent the order and no reason to fear challenging it. Its demands are heavy enough to humiliate, yet the victors, tired of war and divided among themselves, let them be evaded piece by piece, until the settlement has lost both its authority and its power to deter. Much of the interwar story can be told in this way, as a failure less of severity than of follow-through. This is not an argument for cruelty dressed up as realism. Generosity has a real role, but it works best after the defeat has been made unmistakable, when it can be read as the confidence of a winner rather than the hesitation of a power unsure of its victory. Offering a defeated state a path back into the community of nations, through trade, membership of institutions and the eventual lifting of restrictions, gives it a stake in the order that no amount of punishment can create. The point is only that kindness must rest on a settlement that is clear about who won and is backed by someone willing to say so.
R04-E-03: Economic sanctions are usually defended with a simple theory of pressure: cut a country off from markets, credit and imported goods, and its people will suffer; suffering people will blame their rulers; and rulers who fear their own people will eventually change course. Each link in this chain sounds plausible, and the whole has the further appeal of offering governments something to do that is stronger than protest and safer than war, a way of being seen to act without asking anyone to fight. Yet the chain breaks more often than its defenders admit, and it tends to break in the same place. The weak link is the assumption that hardship flows upward as political pressure. In a country whose government controls the press and the police, scarcity is easier to explain than to resist. The regime can present the shortages as the work of hostile foreigners, and the explanation is the more convincing for being partly true. Scarcity also hands the state new powers, which it is seldom slow to use. When imported medicine, fuel or spare parts become rare, whoever controls their distribution acquires a means of rewarding loyalty and punishing dissent. Meanwhile the groups best placed to demand change, the educated and the commercially minded, are often the first to emigrate or to be impoverished into silence. Far from loosening the regime's grip, sanctions can tighten it. The usual response is to make sanctions smarter: to target the assets and travel of named officials rather than the economy as a whole. This is a genuine improvement, since it spares ordinary people some of the cost and aims the pain at those who actually decide. But targeted measures have limits of their own, and those limits are not trivial. Powerful individuals rarely hold their wealth in their own names, and a regime under pressure learns quickly to route its money through intermediaries. Targeting reduces the moral cost of sanctions more reliably than it increases their effect. What the record suggests is that sanctions are often judged by the wrong measure. Their defenders point to the damage done, the fall in output and the collapse of the currency, as if these were evidence of pressure. They are evidence only of pain, and pain is not the same as leverage. Sanctions change policy when they alter the calculations of the people who make it, which usually requires that they be paired with a clear and credible offer of what will be lifted in return for what. A measure that hurts but promises nothing gives a government little reason to move, and some reason to dig in.
R04-E-04: Among the arguments made for nuclear deterrence, the strongest is also the simplest: when two states can each destroy the other, neither can hope to gain from a general war, and so neither starts one. Whatever its moral costs, a balance of terror of this kind has a claim to have kept the largest powers from fighting each other directly for a long time. But the logic that makes the largest war unthinkable may make smaller ones more thinkable, and this possibility, sometimes called the stability-instability paradox, deserves more attention than the reassuring half of the argument usually receives. The reasoning runs as follows. If both sides are confident that neither will ever risk a nuclear exchange, then each can assume that a limited clash, whether a border skirmish, a proxy war or a raid by irregular forces, will stay limited. The fear that once restrained such ventures, the fear that they might spiral into catastrophe, is weakened precisely by the confidence that catastrophe will be avoided. Stability at the top of the ladder of escalation thus loosens the rungs near the bottom. A state that would never dare a full invasion may feel free to probe, provoke and nibble, reasoning that its opponent will not answer with anything that could lead to the unthinkable. It is important to be precise about what this claims. It does not say that nuclear weapons cause small wars, which have many causes and were common long before such weapons existed. It says only that mutual deterrence can lower the perceived risk of low-level aggression and so remove one brake on it. Nor does the paradox operate automatically. Its force depends on how confident each side is that escalation can be controlled. Where leaders doubt that a skirmish can be kept small, the old fear returns, and with it some of the old caution. The implication is uncomfortable for those who credit deterrence with keeping the peace. What deterrence may secure is not peace in general but the absence of one particular kind of war, while the violence that remains is pushed downward and outward, into contested borderlands and into the hands of proxies. That is no small achievement, given what the alternative might be, and nothing in the paradox implies that the world would be safer if the largest powers could once again contemplate fighting each other directly. But the achievement should be described accurately. A system that prevents catastrophe partly by making lesser conflicts safer to start is not a system of peace; it is a way of choosing which wars will be fought.
R04-E-05: The laws of war rest on a premise that, stated baldly, can seem scandalous. A soldier who fights for an aggressor and a soldier who fights to repel him are held to have exactly the same rights on the battlefield: each may lawfully kill enemy combatants, each must spare civilians and prisoners, and neither commits a crime merely by taking part. Whether the war itself was just, a question settled, if at all, by the cause for which it was begun, is treated as irrelevant to how it may be fought. The justice of going to war and justice in the conduct of war are kept in separate compartments, and the ordinary soldier is answerable only for the second. Philosophical critics have pressed hard on this separation, and their central argument is difficult to resist. Outside war, we do not think that someone who attacks without justification acquires a right to kill those who resist him; a robber who is fired on by the guard he is trying to overpower may not shoot back and call it self-defence. Why should the matter change when the attacker wears a uniform and acts on orders? If the right to kill in war derives, as it must, from the right to defend against an unjust threat, then those who pose the unjust threat seem to have no such right at all. On this view, the soldier of an aggressor state who kills a defending soldier does wrong, however scrupulously he observes the rules of conduct. I think the critics are right about the underlying morality and wrong about what follows for the laws of war. Rules for the conduct of hostilities must be followed by people who are frightened, poorly informed and dependent on their own government's account of why they are fighting. Nearly every belligerent believes, or is told, that its cause is just. A rule that granted the right to kill only to soldiers on the just side would therefore be claimed by both sides, and would offer no restraint precisely where restraint is most needed; worse, it would invite each side to treat captured enemies as criminals rather than as prisoners. The symmetry of the laws of war is not a judgement that both sides are equally innocent. It is a convention adopted because the alternative would make war more savage without making it more just. Conceding this does not license the conclusion that soldiers bear no responsibility for the wars they fight. A convention that withholds legal blame is not a certificate of moral innocence, and there will be wars whose injustice is so plain that an ordinary soldier could see it and ought to refuse. The doctrine of equality is best understood not as a truth about the morality of killing but as a practical arrangement that we maintain, knowingly, because it does more to limit the horror of war than any rule that tracked the moral truth more closely could do.
R04-E-06: Collective security is one of those ideas that seem obviously right until one asks what they require. The principle is that an attack on any member of an international system is to be treated as an attack on all, so that every aggressor faces the combined strength of everyone else. Against this, the older practice of the balance of power looks cynical: states align against whichever power threatens to dominate, and they change sides as readily as the threat shifts, guided by interest rather than by any judgement about who is in the right. The appeal of collective security lies in its impartiality, and so does its weakness. For the scheme to work, states must be willing to fight an aggressor regardless of who it is, which means fighting, if necessary, a friend, a major trading partner or a power whose goodwill they need elsewhere. They must also be willing to fight over places where they have no interest at all, because the principle admits no distinction between an attack that matters to them and one that does not. This is a great deal to ask of governments that answer to their own citizens, and the interwar experience suggests that, when the moment came, many would not pay the price. An organisation founded on the principle found its members ready to condemn aggression and reluctant to resist it. The balance of power asks less and so delivers more reliably, at least within its narrower aims. It does not require states to care about aggression as such, only about the rise of a power that could threaten them, and so it draws on motives that governments actually have. But its reliability comes at a price. Because it attends only to the distribution of strength, it is indifferent to the fate of small states whose conquest does not upset the balance; it can tolerate, and has often arranged, the partition of a weak country as a way of keeping the strong ones satisfied. Stability is its aim, and justice enters only by accident. The lesson is not that one principle should replace the other, but that each supplies what the other lacks. A norm against aggression, however imperfectly enforced, gives resistance to an expanding power a public justification and makes it easier to assemble allies who would hesitate to act on calculation alone. Balancing, in turn, supplies the motive that the norm cannot generate by itself. Orders that have lasted have usually combined the two, borrowing their legitimacy from the first and their enforcement from the second, and the mistake of the reformers who championed collective security was to imagine that legitimacy could do the work of both.
R04-E-07: For much of the modern period the doctrine of sovereignty was understood as a wall. Within its borders a state was answerable to no outside authority, and what it did to its own population, however terrible, was a matter of domestic jurisdiction. The rule had a defensible rationale. A world in which any power could enter another's territory whenever it disapproved of how that territory was governed would be a world of permanent intervention, in which the strong would always find reasons to correct the weak. Non-interference was less a tribute to the virtue of governments than a device for keeping their quarrels within bounds. The atrocities of the late twentieth century made the wall look like a shield for murderers, and a new formula emerged to reconcile the old principle with the demand to act. Sovereignty, it was argued, is not a privilege but a responsibility: a state holds it on condition that it protects its people, and a state that massacres them, or cannot stop others from doing so, forfeits its claim to be left alone. The formula is elegant, because it seems to dissolve the conflict rather than adjudicate it. Intervention to stop mass killing no longer violates sovereignty, since the sovereignty in question has already been forfeited. The elegance is partly an illusion. The formula does not remove the hard question but relocates it. Someone must still decide when a government has failed badly enough to forfeit its rights, and in practice that someone is usually the state or coalition proposing to intervene, which is to say a party with interests of its own in the outcome. The old doctrine at least gave a clear answer to the question of who may enter: nobody. The new one replaces that answer with a judgement, and judgements made by the powerful about the weak have a history that should make anyone cautious. It is not a cynical point that intervention has tended to occur where the interveners had strategic reasons to be and not elsewhere; it is an observation about how a discretionary rule will be used. None of this is an argument for returning to the wall. A principle that obliged the world to watch a massacre it could stop would purchase order at a price few would accept once they had seen what it meant. The question is not whether sovereignty may ever yield, but how the decision that it should yield is to be made credible. Here the procedure matters as much as the facts. An intervention authorised by a broad body of states, through rules that apply to friends as well as to enemies, carries a legitimacy that one undertaken by a single power on its own assessment cannot, even when the atrocities alleged are equally real. The difficulty is that procedure can fail in the other direction. The bodies most able to confer legitimacy are also those in which a single interested member can block action, and the insistence on proper authorisation can become a reason for doing nothing while the killing continues. There is no formula that escapes this. A world that refuses all unauthorised intervention will sometimes stand by when it should act, and a world that permits it will sometimes see intervention used as a pretext. The honest position is to admit that we are choosing which of these failures to risk, and to stop pretending that a change of vocabulary has spared us the choice.
R04-E-08: Every alliance contains a quiet bargain between two fears. A state that joins an alliance worries, on the one hand, that its partner will fail it when it is attacked: this is the fear of abandonment. It worries, on the other, that its partner will drag it into a war it has no wish to fight, over interests that are not its own: this is the fear of entrapment. The two fears pull in opposite directions, and much of what passes for the routine management of alliances, the ministerial visits, the joint statements, the careful wording of guarantees, is an effort to keep them in tolerable balance. The difficulty is that almost anything done to ease one fear aggravates the other. A state that tightens its commitment, by stationing troops on its partner's soil or promising automatic assistance, reassures the partner that it will not be abandoned. But the same assurance may embolden the partner to take risks it would otherwise avoid, confident that its ally will be obliged to follow. Loosening the commitment has the opposite effect: it restrains the partner, but it also invites the partner to doubt the alliance and perhaps to look for other friends, or to arm in ways that alarm its neighbours. There is no setting of the dial at which both fears disappear, and governments that search for one tend to lurch between them, reassuring an anxious ally one year and reining in an emboldened one the next. For this reason, the ambiguity of many alliance commitments, often criticised as a failure of nerve, is better seen as a deliberate instrument. A guarantee that is firm enough to deter an adversary but vague about the circumstances in which it will be honoured leaves the protecting power room to judge whether its partner has provoked the crisis. The partner, uncertain whether reckless conduct will be supported, has reason to be careful; the adversary, uncertain whether aggression will be resisted, has reason to be careful too. Consider a hypothetical great power that promises to defend an island partner but declines to say whether the promise covers a dispute the partner itself might start. The silence is not an oversight. It is the policy. The balance between the two fears is rarely the same for both members. A small state facing a powerful neighbour usually fears abandonment far more than entrapment, since it has few other places to turn, while its larger protector, with interests elsewhere and wars it would prefer not to fight, tends to fear entrapment more. Much of the friction within alliances that look harmonious from outside comes from this asymmetry: the junior partner asks for firmer pledges, the senior partner resists giving them, and each suspects the other of bad faith when each is in fact responding sensibly to its own position. Ambiguity is not free, however. Its value depends on each party reading the uncertainty in the way the protecting power intends, and there is no guarantee that they will. An adversary may conclude that a vague commitment is a hollow one and test it, discovering too late that it was real. A partner may conclude that it will be supported whatever it does, because it cannot imagine its patron allowing it to fall. Deliberate vagueness thus trades the visible risks of a firm commitment for the hidden risk of miscalculation, which is the more dangerous for being invisible until a crisis reveals it. The strategy rewards a protecting power that understands both its partner and its adversary well, and punishes one that merely hopes it does.
